questions.question: What is the domain of $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ as given?
options: $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$

questions.question: What is the domain of $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ as given?
options: $\mathbb{R}$
$\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$

questions.question: Why is a function only evaluated on its domain?
options: Because its domain is always $\mathbb{R}$.
Because a function is only defined on its domain.
Because the domain contains only outputs.
Because the domain must be finite.

questions.question: Can two functions share the same formula yet be different functions?
options: No: a formula fixes its natural domain, so it determines the function.
Yes: the same formula on different domains gives different functions.
Yes, but only when the formulas use different variable names.
Yes: one formula on one domain can still give two different ranges.

questions.question: If $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$, which input is not allowed?
If $g(x) = \sqrt{x}$, which input belongs to the given domain?
A formula such as $1/x$ is displayed without specifying allowed inputs. Which mistake does this invite?
options: Assuming every function has an empty domain.
Assuming the domain is always a single number.
Assuming the displayed formula alone fixes the function without specifying allowed inputs.
Assuming the domain is the set of output values the formula $1/x$ can produce, rather than its inputs.

questions.question: Which kind of condition can impose restrictions on the domain of a function?
options: Only the colour of the graph
Algebraic or analytical conditions
Only the name of the variable
Only whether the function is drawn by hand

questions.question: Consider the formula $h(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ with proposed domain $\mathbb{R}$. What is the problem?
options: The input $1$ is included, but $\frac{1}{x}$ is not defined at $1$.
The domain must be $[0,+\infty)$ for every function.
The domain contains too few real numbers.
The input $0$ is included, but $\frac{1}{x}$ is not defined at $0$.

questions.question: Two functions both have formula $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$, but one has domain $[0,+\infty)$ and the other has domain $[1,+\infty)$. What should we say?
options: They are the same function because the formula is written the same way.
They are different functions because their domains differ.
The second one is not a function because its domain is smaller.
The first one has no domain.

questions.question: What does the domain specify?
options: Which output values are attained.
Which input values are allowed.
Only the largest output value.
The colour of the graph.

questions.question: A function is only defined where?
options: Only on its range.
Outside its domain.
On its domain.
Only at zero.

questions.question: Why can two identical formulas define different functions?
options: They may have different domains.
They must have different names.
They must have the same range.
They cannot have any inputs.

questions.question: What kinds of conditions can restrict a domain?
options: Only the name of the function.
Only whether the output is rational.
Only the number of letters in the formula.
Algebraic or analytical conditions.
